senses.gloss: Connected with machines or the way they work.
examples: The flight was delayed by a *mechanical* problem.
She studied *mechanical* engineering.
The old clock is purely *mechanical* — there is no battery in it.

senses.gloss: Done automatically, without thought or feeling.
examples: He gave a *mechanical* nod and kept reading.
Her apology sounded *mechanical*.

senses.gloss: Using machines in place of people or animals.
examples: Most of the harvest is now fully *mechanized*.
The army sent in a *mechanized* infantry unit.
Sorting the mail used to be done by hand; today it is *mechanized*.

ru: назойливый, лезущий не в своё дело

senses.gloss: Always interfering in other people's business.
senses.ru: назойливый, вмешивающийся не в своё дело
examples: His *meddlesome* aunt rearranged the whole kitchen.
Reporters called the agency *meddlesome* and slow.
She has a *meddlesome* streak, but she means well.

senses.gloss: Interfering in things that are none of your business.
examples: He blamed *meddling* bureaucrats for the delay.
Her *meddling* neighbors report every car on the street.
The play is about a *meddling* mother-in-law.

contrast: The *median* is the middle value, not the average: half the numbers fall below it. The average is the *mean*.

senses.gloss: In the middle of a set of values, with half above and half below.
examples: *Median* household income rose by two percent.
*Median* home prices fell for the first time in a decade.
The *median* age in the town is forty-one.

position: both — nearly always before a noun

senses.gloss: Connected with medicine and the treatment of illness.
examples: She is in her second year of *medical* school.
The company covers *medical* expenses.
The cause of the fainting turned out to be *medical*, not stress.

contrast: *Medicinal* is about healing power; *medical* is about doctors and hospitals.

senses.gloss: Used as medicine, or having the effect of medicine.
examples: The plant has *medicinal* properties.
He keeps a bottle of whiskey for *medicinal* purposes.
The tea was bitter and faintly *medicinal*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Middle Ages, roughly 500 to 1500.
examples: The town has a *medieval* cathedral.
She teaches *medieval* history.

senses.gloss: Harsh and old-fashioned, used to criticize.
examples: Their attitude toward women is frankly *medieval*.
Conditions in the prison were *medieval*.

senses.gloss: Not bad, but clearly not good — only average.
examples: The food was *mediocre* and the service was slow.
He had a *mediocre* season and lost his place on the team.
The movie is *mediocre* at best.

senses.gloss: Quiet and thoughtful, or making you feel that way.
examples: He was in a *meditative* mood all evening.
The music is slow and *meditative*.
She sat by the window with a *meditative* look on her face.

contrast: Always capitalized. As a noun, *the Mediterranean* is the sea itself.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Mediterranean Sea and the countries around it.
examples: We ate at a *Mediterranean* restaurant downtown.
The house has a *Mediterranean* feel, with white walls and blue shutters.
The climate here is *Mediterranean*: hot dry summers and mild winters.

contrast: Also a noun: a *medium* is a means of communication, or a person who claims to speak with the dead. The plural of the first is *media*.

senses.gloss: Between large and small, or halfway between two extremes.
examples: I'll take a *medium* coffee.
She is of *medium* height.
He has *medium* brown hair.

senses.gloss: Of meat: cooked so that the inside is still slightly pink.
examples: I ordered my steak *medium*.
He likes his burgers *medium* rather than well done.

senses.gloss: Neither large nor small.
examples: They live in a *medium-sized* town in Ohio.
Chop two *medium-sized* onions.
It is a *medium-sized* firm with about sixty employees.

senses.gloss: Quiet and gentle, and unwilling to argue or stand up for yourself.
examples: She is too *meek* to complain about the noise.
He offered a *meek* apology and sat down.
With every year he grew *meeker* and quieter.

senses.gloss: Obsessed with your own power and greatness.
examples: The film's villain is a *megalomaniacal* tech billionaire.
His plans grew more *megalomaniacal* with every meeting.
Critics called the whole project *megalomaniacal*.

senses.gloss: Sad in a quiet, lasting way.
examples: The songs are slow and *melancholic*.
He gets *melancholic* every November.
There is a *melancholic* beauty to the empty beach.

contrast: Also a noun: *a deep melancholy settled over him*. After a verb, *melancholic* is more common.

senses.gloss: Full of quiet sadness.
examples: She played a *melancholy* tune on the piano.
The letter has a *melancholy* tone.
He was in a *melancholy* mood after the funeral.

senses.gloss: Smooth and pleasant to listen to.
examples: The announcer has a *mellifluous* voice.
Her prose is *mellifluous* and easy to read aloud.
He sang the last verse in a low, *mellifluous* tone.

senses.gloss: Calm and relaxed, and not easily upset.
examples: He has gotten *mellower* since he retired.
It was a *mellow* Sunday afternoon.

senses.gloss: Soft and rich — of a sound, a light, a taste or a color.
examples: The wine is smooth and *mellow*.
A *mellow* light came through the curtains.

senses.gloss: Having a pleasant tune, or having to do with melody.
examples: The band's new album is more *melodic* than the last one.
She writes the *melodic* line first and the words later.
His voice is deep and *melodic*.

contrast: *Melodious* describes a sound that is pleasant; *melodic* also covers anything to do with melody (*the melodic line*).

senses.gloss: Pleasant to hear; full of melody.
examples: A *melodious* birdsong woke us at dawn.
Her laugh is low and *melodious*.
The choir sounded *melodious* even without the organ.

senses.gloss: Showing far more emotion than the situation deserves.
examples: Don't be so *melodramatic* — it's only a scratch.
The ending is *melodramatic*, but the acting saves it.
She made a *melodramatic* exit, slamming the door behind her.

contrast: *Melted* is the finished state (*melted butter*); *molten* is used for metal and rock that is hot and liquid (*molten lava*).

senses.gloss: Turned into liquid by heat.
examples: Pour the *melted* butter over the popcorn.
The sandwich comes with *melted* cheese.
By noon the snow was *melted* and the streets were wet.

senses.gloss: Worth remembering, or easy to remember.
examples: It was a *memorable* evening.
The speech was short but *memorable*.
Few songs are as *memorable* as that one.

senses.gloss: Looking or sounding as if harm is coming.
examples: A *menacing* dog stood at the gate.
The sky turned dark and *menacing*.
He took a step forward and said something in a *menacing* voice.

senses.gloss: Of work: boring, low-paid and seen as having little status.
examples: He took a *menial* job to pay for school.
New interns get the most *menial* tasks.
She was tired of *menial* work and went back to college.

senses.gloss: Connected with menopause, the end of a woman's monthly periods.
examples: She is being treated for *menopausal* symptoms.
The study followed two hundred *menopausal* women.
Hot flashes are a common *menopausal* complaint.

senses.gloss: Connected with the monthly bleeding of a woman's body.
examples: Her *menstrual* cycle is very regular.
The app tracks *menstrual* symptoms.
*Menstrual* cramps kept her home from school.

contrast: In American English *mental* is not used to mean *crazy* — that is British slang.

senses.gloss: Connected with the mind and how it works.
examples: *Mental* health is finally being taken seriously.
He did the whole calculation in his head — pure *mental* arithmetic.

senses.gloss: Existing in the mind rather than on paper.
examples: I made a *mental* note to call her back.
She keeps a *mental* list of everything the kids need.

comparison: not gradable — degree goes in the adverb: *severely mentally ill*
contrast: As a group noun it takes *the* and a plural verb: *the mentally ill are often homeless*. Many writers now prefer *people with mental illness*.

senses.gloss: Suffering from an illness of the mind.
examples: He was found to be *mentally ill* and sent for treatment.
The shelter serves homeless and *mentally ill* adults.
She is not *mentally ill*; she is exhausted.

contrast: Also a noun: a *mercenary* is a soldier who fights for whoever pays him.

senses.gloss: Interested only in money, not in doing what is right.
examples: His motives were purely *mercenary*.
Critics accused the studio of *mercenary* decisions.
There is something *mercenary* about the way he picks his friends.

senses.gloss: Willing to forgive, or to spare someone pain or punishment.
examples: The judge was *merciful* and gave him probation.
Be *merciful* to the ones who made an honest mistake.

senses.gloss: Of an event: a relief, because it ends something painful.
examples: His death was quick and *merciful*.
After ten days of heat, the rain was *merciful*.

senses.gloss: Showing no pity at all.
examples: The teasing at school was *merciless*.
She is a *merciless* editor — half my draft is gone.
The August sun was *merciless*.

senses.gloss: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and often.
examples: The coach is brilliant but *mercurial*.
Her *mercurial* temper kept the whole office on edge.
Stock prices have been *mercurial* all week.

senses.gloss: Based on ability and effort rather than on money or family.
examples: The company claims to have a *meritocratic* promotion system.
Admissions are supposed to be *meritocratic*.
He argues the country is less *meritocratic* than it pretends.

contrast: Outside *Merry Christmas* and a few set phrases, Americans say *cheerful* or *happy*.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and full of good spirits.
examples: *Merry* Christmas and a happy New Year!
A *merry* crowd filled the square.
The more people come, the *merrier* the party.

contrast: *Mesmerized* is the person; *mesmerizing* is the thing that does it to them.

senses.gloss: Unable to look away or think about anything else.
examples: The kids sat *mesmerized* in front of the fire.
I was *mesmerized* by her voice.
He watched the waves, completely *mesmerized*.

contrast: Pairs with *mesmerized*: the film is *mesmerizing*, so the audience is *mesmerized*.

senses.gloss: So beautiful or strange that you cannot look away.
examples: The dancer was *mesmerizing*.
It is a *mesmerizing* film about life at sea.
There is something *mesmerizing* about watching bread rise.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you had been chosen to save everyone.
examples: He talks about the company with *messianic* zeal.
The movement took on a *messianic* tone.

senses.gloss: Connected with the Messiah in religion.
examples: The professor writes about *messianic* prophecy.
*Messianic* expectations ran high in the first century.

senses.gloss: Dirty, or not in any order.
examples: His room is *messier* than mine.
Sorry, the kitchen is a little *messy* right now.

senses.gloss: Complicated and unpleasant to deal with.
examples: They went through a *messy* divorce.
The negotiations got *messy*.

senses.gloss: Connected with the chemical processes that keep a body alive.
examples: She was diagnosed with a rare *metabolic* disorder.
Exercise raises your *metabolic* rate.
The drug affects *metabolic* function in the liver.

senses.gloss: Using an image to mean something else; not meant literally.
examples: The wall he keeps talking about is *metaphorical*, not made of bricks.
It was a *metaphorical* way of saying he was worn out.
Her poems are dense and *metaphorical*.

senses.gloss: Concerned with what exists and what is real, beyond the physical world.
examples: The book asks *metaphysical* questions about time and the self.
We got into a long *metaphysical* argument at dinner.
The problem is practical, not *metaphysical*.

contrast: Almost always in *a meteoric rise*: fast and bright, never falling.

senses.gloss: Of success: very fast and spectacular.
examples: Her *meteoric* rise took her from intern to partner in six years.
The band's *meteoric* success surprised everyone, including the band.
After a *meteoric* start, the company ran out of money.

senses.gloss: Connected with the weather and the study of it.
examples: The delay was caused by *meteorological* conditions.
He works at a *meteorological* station in Alaska.
*Meteorological* records here go back to 1890.

senses.gloss: Doing things in a careful, ordered way, one step at a time.
examples: She is *methodical* about everything, from packing to paying bills.
The search was slow and *methodical*.
He keeps *methodical* notes on every patient.

contrast: Always capitalized. Also a noun: *she was raised a Methodist*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Methodist branch of the Protestant church.
examples: They were married in a *Methodist* church.
His grandfather was a *Methodist* minister.
The town has a small *Methodist* congregation.

contrast: *Methodological* is about the method of a study; *methodical* is about a careful person.

senses.gloss: Connected with the methods used in research or work.
examples: The paper has serious *methodological* problems.
Reviewers raised *methodological* objections.
One *methodological* change gave them a completely different result.

senses.gloss: Very careful about small details.
examples: He is *meticulous* about his tools.
The restoration took years of *meticulous* work.
She kept *meticulous* records of every dollar spent.

contrast: Also a noun in business English: a *metric* is a number you measure success by.

senses.gloss: Using meters, grams and liters.
examples: Most of the world uses the *metric* system.
The recipe gives *metric* measurements.
A *metric* ton is a thousand kilograms.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a large city and the area around it.
examples: Three million people live in the *metropolitan* area.
The *metropolitan* police handled the case.
*Metropolitan* voters went the other way.

senses.gloss: Concerned with single firms, households and markets rather than the whole economy.
examples: The paper takes a *microeconomic* approach to health care.
*Microeconomic* theory starts with supply and demand.
She teaches a *microeconomic* analysis course.

senses.gloss: Far too small to see without a microscope.
examples: *Microscopic* cracks had appeared in the metal.
The water is full of *microscopic* life.

senses.gloss: Extremely small, in everyday exaggeration.
examples: They served us *microscopic* portions.
The chance of winning is *microscopic*.

contrast: In American use it means the states from New York down to Virginia, not the middle of the ocean.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the middle part of the US Atlantic coast.
examples: Snow is expected across the *Mid-Atlantic* states.
She grew up in a *Mid-Atlantic* suburb.
The chain has thirty *Mid-Atlantic* stores.

contrast: The adjective only goes before a noun. After a verb use the noun: *The house is in the middle of the block*, never *the house is middle*.

senses.gloss: In the center, between two other things or points.
examples: She is the *middle* child of three.
Put the box on the *middle* shelf.
We met in *middle* school.

contrast: Both words are capitalized, and there is no hyphen.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the countries of the Middle East.
examples: They opened a *Middle Eastern* restaurant downtown.
He covers *Middle Eastern* politics for the paper.
The spice blend is distinctly *Middle Eastern*.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun; as a noun phrase it is two words: *the middle class is shrinking*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the group of people between the rich and the poor.
examples: They grew up in a comfortable *middle-class* neighborhood.
The bill offers a tax cut to *middle-class* families.
She writes about *middle-class* anxiety.

form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Moderate; avoiding either extreme, especially in politics or taste.
examples: He ran as a *middle-of-the-road* Democrat.
The station plays *middle-of-the-road* pop.
Her views are pretty *middle-of-the-road*.

contrast: Often in the set phrase *fair to middling*, meaning so-so.

senses.gloss: Of only average quality or size — neither good nor bad.
examples: The movie got *middling* reviews.
He had a *middling* career and retired quietly.
The team is coming off a *middling* season.

contrast: Capitalized. The region is *the Midwest*; a person from there is a *Midwesterner*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Midwest of the United States.
examples: She has a flat *Midwestern* accent.
The company started in a small *Midwestern* town.
His politeness is very *Midwestern*.

contrast: Informal and mild — being *miffed* is much weaker than being *angry*.

senses.gloss: Slightly annoyed, usually at being left out or overlooked.
examples: She was *miffed* that nobody told her about the meeting.
He looked a little *miffed* at being asked to wait.
I was *miffed* about the seating, but I got over it.

contrast: In the South and in older writing *mighty* is also an adverb meaning *very* (*mighty fine*). That is not the adjective.

senses.gloss: Very strong and powerful.
examples: The *mighty* Mississippi runs past the town.
The pen is *mightier* than the sword.
He swung at the ball with a *mighty* effort.

contrast: Far more common as a noun (*migrants crossed the border*); the adjective only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Moving from place to place, especially in search of work.
examples: *Migrant* workers pick most of the state's fruit.
The county opened a clinic for *migrant* families.
The film follows a *migrant* family across three states.

senses.gloss: Regularly moving from one region to another with the seasons.
examples: The lake is a stop for *migratory* birds.
*Migratory* patterns have shifted with the warmer winters.
Some of these whales are *migratory*; others stay all year.

senses.gloss: Not strong and not severe.
examples: He had a *mild* case of the flu.
This winter is *milder* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Of food: not hot or spicy.
examples: I'll take the *mild* salsa, please.
The cheese is *mild* and creamy.

senses.gloss: Of a person: gentle and not easily angered.
examples: He is a *mild* man who never raises his voice.
She answered in a *mild* tone.

senses.gloss: Quiet and gentle in the way you deal with people.
examples: He is a *mild-mannered* accountant from Ohio.
Our *mild-mannered* neighbor turned out to be a champion boxer.
She is *mild-mannered* until you insult her cooking.

contrast: Also a noun: *militants attacked the base*.

senses.gloss: Willing to use forceful or violent methods for a cause.
examples: A *militant* faction split off from the party.
He became more *militant* after the strike failed.
She is a *militant* defender of public libraries.

senses.gloss: Believing a country should build up its army and be ready to use it.
examples: The regime grew steadily more *militaristic*.
Textbooks described the empire as *militaristic*.
He objects to the *militaristic* tone of the ceremony.

senses.gloss: Supplied with soldiers, weapons or military methods.
examples: The border has become heavily *militarized*.
Critics say local police are too *militarized*.
They crossed a *militarized* zone to reach the camp.

contrast: Also a noun: *the military* means the armed forces and always takes *the*.

senses.gloss: Connected with soldiers and the armed forces.
examples: He spent four years in *military* service.
The base is under *military* control.
*Military* families move often.

senses.gloss: Pale white and not clear, like milk.
examples: The stone turns *milky* when it gets wet.
A *milky* haze hung over the bay.

senses.gloss: Containing or tasting of milk.
examples: She likes her tea *milky*.
The sauce came out *milkier* than I expected.

contrast: Two *l*s and two *n*s. Also a noun: *millennials* are people born roughly between 1981 and 1996.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the generation born in the 1980s and 1990s.
examples: The ad is aimed at *millennial* shoppers.
Her taste in music is very *millennial*.

senses.gloss: Connected with a period of a thousand years.
examples: The cathedral held a *millennial* celebration.
He writes about *millennial* prophecies.

senses.gloss: Changing the way your mind works — of a drug or an experience.
examples: The study looked at *mind-altering* drugs.
He described the trip as a *mind-altering* experience.
Some *mind-altering* substances are legal in the state.

senses.gloss: So strange or complicated that it is hard to take in.
examples: The last episode has a *mind-bending* twist.
The math involved is frankly *mind-bending*.
It is a *mind-bending* movie that rewards a second viewing.

contrast: Informal, and usually praise. *Mind-boggling* is about size or confusion instead.

senses.gloss: Amazing; far beyond what you expected.
examples: The view from the top is *mind-blowing*.
She gave a *mind-blowing* performance.
The price of housing here is *mind-blowing*.

senses.gloss: So large or complicated that you cannot really imagine it.
examples: The numbers are *mind-boggling*: nine billion dollars a year.
It took a *mind-boggling* amount of paperwork.
The scale of the project is *mind-boggling*.

senses.gloss: Keeping something in mind; aware of it.
examples: Be *mindful* of the step on your way out.
She spoke slowly, *mindful* that children were listening.

senses.gloss: Paying calm, deliberate attention to the present moment.
examples: He practices *mindful* breathing every morning.
The clinic teaches *mindful* eating.

senses.gloss: Needing no thought, or done without any.
examples: After work I want some *mindless* television.
The job is *mindless*, but it pays.

senses.gloss: Senseless and violent, with no reason behind it.
examples: The riot was *mindless* destruction.
Police called it a *mindless* attack.

contrast: Also a noun (*iron is a mineral*); as an adjective it only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Made of minerals, or containing them.
examples: She drinks sparkling *mineral* water.
The state sold the *mineral* rights to the land.
*Mineral* deposits line the inside of the kettle.

contrast: Also a noun: *a portrait painted in miniature*.

senses.gloss: Much smaller than usual, but the same in every other way.
examples: He collects *miniature* trains.
They keep a *miniature* poodle.
The museum has a *miniature* version of the whole city.

senses.gloss: As small as possible; very little.
examples: The damage to the car was *minimal*.
The treatment has *minimal* side effects.
We finished with *minimal* help from the main office.

contrast: Also a noun: *she is a minimalist*.

senses.gloss: Using very few and very simple elements.
examples: The apartment has a *minimalist* design — a bed, a lamp, nothing else.
His style is deliberately *minimalist*.
They gave the album a *minimalist* cover.

contrast: Also a noun: *a minimum of three years*. The fixed phrase is *minimum wage*, never *minimal wage*.

senses.gloss: The smallest that is allowed or required.
examples: He works two jobs at *minimum* wage.
There is a *minimum* age of eighteen.
The order carries a *minimum* charge of twenty dollars.

contrast: Also a noun: a *minor* is a person under eighteen. In music the word follows the note: *A minor*.

senses.gloss: Small and not very important or serious.
examples: She had a *minor* injury and played the next day.
There are a few *minor* changes to the schedule.
The problem is *minor* compared with what we faced last year.

contrast: Also a noun — the plant, the candy, and the place where coins are made. The flavor adjective is *minty*, not *mint*.

senses.gloss: In perfect, unused condition, as if just made.
examples: The comic is in *mint* condition.
He bought a *mint* 1965 Mustang.
Collectors pay extra for a *mint* copy.

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling of mint.
examples: The toothpaste has a strong *minty* taste.
She made a cool, *minty* drink.
This gum is *mintier* than the other brand.

contrast: Spelled *minu-*, not *mini-*, even though *miniscule* is now common in print.

senses.gloss: Extremely small.
examples: The print on the contract is *minuscule*.
He got a *minuscule* raise.
The risk of that happening is *minuscule*.

contrast: The adjective is my-NOOT; the noun *minute* (sixty seconds) is MIN-it. Same spelling, different word.

senses.gloss: Very small indeed.
examples: *Minute* traces of the metal were found in the water.
The difference between the two samples is *minute*.

senses.gloss: Going into the smallest details.
examples: She described the room in *minute* detail.
The report gives a *minute* account of the accident.

senses.gloss: So lucky or surprising that it seems like a miracle.
examples: She made a *miraculous* recovery.
It is *miraculous* that nobody was hurt.
The team's comeback was nothing short of *miraculous*.

senses.gloss: Stuck in a bad situation you cannot get out of.
examples: The bill is *mired* in committee.
The company is *mired* in debt.
For two years the project was *mired* in lawsuits.

senses.gloss: Covered with mirrors, or made of mirror glass.
examples: The gym has one *mirrored* wall.
He wore *mirrored* sunglasses.
The tower's *mirrored* windows reflect the whole skyline.

senses.gloss: Disliking people in general and avoiding them.
examples: He has grown *misanthropic* since he moved to the cabin.
The novel's narrator is funny and deeply *misanthropic*.
She is not *misanthropic*, just tired of small talk.

senses.gloss: Of many different kinds, grouped together because they fit nowhere else.
examples: The drawer is full of *miscellaneous* junk.
*Miscellaneous* expenses came to sixty dollars.
She filed the letters under *miscellaneous* correspondence.

contrast: Three syllables, MIS-chi-vuhs — not *mis-CHEE-vee-uhs* — and spelled *-vous*, not *-vious*.

senses.gloss: Enjoying causing small amounts of trouble, in a playful way.
examples: He gave her a *mischievous* grin.
The puppy is *mischievous* but harmless.
She had a *mischievous* streak as a child.

senses.gloss: Extremely unhappy or uncomfortable.
examples: She was *miserable* the whole first year at the new school.
I had a cold and felt *miserable*.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant — of weather or conditions.
examples: It was a *miserable* November day, cold and wet.
They played the whole game in *miserable* conditions.

form: -ly from the noun *miser* — an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: *Miserly* ends in *-ly* but is an adjective, like *friendly* and *lovely*.

senses.gloss: Hating to spend money.
examples: His *miserly* uncle heated only one room of the house.
She is careful with money; he is simply *miserly*.

senses.gloss: Of an amount: much too small.
examples: The raise was a *miserly* one percent.
They offered a *miserly* two days off.

senses.gloss: Based on bad judgment or wrong information, though usually well meant.
examples: It was a *misguided* attempt to help.
He is sincere but badly *misguided*.
The policy was *misguided* from the start.

senses.gloss: Given the wrong name or description on its label.
examples: The jars were *mislabeled* and had to be pulled from the shelves.
He bought a *mislabeled* bottle of olive oil.
One *mislabeled* file cost us two days.

senses.gloss: Giving a wrong idea, whether on purpose or not.
examples: The ad was found to be *misleading*.
That chart is *misleading* because the scale starts at fifty.
He gave a *misleading* answer about where he had been.

senses.gloss: Not going together well; wrongly paired.
examples: He showed up in *mismatched* socks.
The two fighters were badly *mismatched*.
The furniture is *mismatched*, but somehow it works.
